The organisations will foster mutual learning amongst themselves and the other consortium and advocacy partners on intersecting issues, movement building and advocacy with organisations in West Africa and the MENA region through partner exchange visits and learning events

Sex Worker Education and Advocacy Taskforce (SWEAT)

activity-date.narrative: The National Sex Work Plan for HIV, TB, and STIs (2019-2022) was launched in October 2021, signalling progress toward decriminalization, as evidenced by its frequent mention in the document. In 2021, South Africa’s Department of Justice began reviewing the Sexual Offences Amendment Act, with Sisonke submitting recommendations advocating for decriminalization. Additionally, Sisonke contributed to the Hate Crime Bill to combat violence and discrimination against sex workers. Throughout the year, government and civil society held dialogues to address sex workers’ access to justice, healthcare, and human rights. Sisonke strengthened its efforts by appointing new staff and collaborating with organizations representing key populations, such as people who use drugs, LGBTQI+ individuals, and PLHIV. Partnerships with groups like Show Me Your Number led to community radio shows on human rights and SRHR. During COVID-19, Sisonke worked with NAPWA to ensure sex workers received HIV treatment. The Decriminalisation Working Group is engaging with the Department of Justice to amend laws and draft a decriminalization bill, consulting sex workers nationwide. Provincial structures have been formalized to enhance sex worker representation in decision-making. Sisonke organizes workshops on stigma, discrimination, and gender-based violence, empowering sex workers to document rights violations and access legal support. The Dignity Diversity Policing (DDP) training, conducted with partners like Triangle Project and SANPUD, educates law enforcement on reducing brutality against sex workers, LGBTQI+ individuals, and drug users. Sisonke’s annual national meeting brings together sex workers from all provinces to discuss challenges and progress toward decriminalization. Outreach programs link sex workers to healthcare, including ART and SRHR services, while monitoring rights violations. The KwaZulu-Natal adoption of the National Sex Work Plan, endorsed by government officials, marks a significant step. A multisectoral approach ensures advocacy efforts address intersecting stigmas faced by different key populations. Innovations like WhatsApp groups, online campaigns, and webinars have expanded engagement, fostering collaboration and faster dissemination of advocacy initiatives. In 2022, Sisonke trained its ReActors and Human Rights Defenders in lobbying strategies, documentation of rights violations, and engaging local decision-makers, strengthening advocacy for law reform. These efforts extended to outreach, where beneficiaries were educated on their rights. As the coordinator of South African grantees, Sisonke hosted monthly meetings to foster collaboration and address advocacy gaps among key populations (KPs). Engagement with the Love Alliance Working Groups provided insights into global advocacy, while consultations on the Policy Scoping Review highlighted research gaps, such as insufficient data on transgender individuals and young people, as well as underfunding of community-led organizations. A major milestone was the Decriminalisation Symposium, which brought together grantees, KPs, and the public to discuss barriers to health and justice, reinforcing collective advocacy efforts.A significant national development was the launch of South Africa’s Gender-Based Violence and Femicide (GBV-F) Plan, where President Ramaphosa declared GBV a "second pandemic." Crucially, the plan explicitly calls for sex work decriminalization—a major advocacy victory. Sisonke and civil society must now monitor implementation. Additionally, government dialogues, such as the Northern Cape engagement with the Department of Social Development, addressed GBV’s impact on marginalized groups, with activists highlighting the urgent need for sex workers’ rights. In court cases, Sisonke mobilized support for victims, including assisting families in identifying murdered sex workers and ensuring proper legal processes. Partner organizations like Access Chapter 2 helped KPs understand court procedures, empowering them to demand justice.The Decriminalisation Working Group intensified lobbying efforts, consulting sex workers nationwide to shape the draft bill, emphasizing equal access to justice and healthcare. South African Love Alliance grantees developed a unified advocacy strategy focusing on law reform, drug policy, media accountability, and inclusive education. Lobbying trainings equipped Human Rights Defenders and Peer Educators with skills to engage government structures, while photography workshops (in partnership with Market Photo Workshop) provided KPs a creative outlet to depict stigma and discrimination. A Decriminalisation Webinar for International Sex Workers Day examined global progress and the intersection of law reform and healthcare access.Sisonke conducted SRHR workshops in six provinces, documenting challenges in healthcare access, such as long queues and lack of mobile clinics. A critical issue was food insecurity affecting medication adherence, prompting plans to collaborate with SANCO and the Department of Social Development. The workshops reinforced sex workers’ rights to safe, satisfying sexual health, including access to contraception and STI prevention. These efforts, alongside partnerships with health organizations, aim to ensure equitable services for all KPs, advancing both health and human rights.A 2023 survey and focus group discussions in the Western Cape gathered qualitative data on young sex workers’ SRHR challenges and rights violations. This research will inform a 2024 Leadership Training Manual to better address sex workers' needs. Creative spaces also played a crucial role, with sex workers using storytelling and art to raise awareness on SRHR, gender-based violence (GBV), and human rights. These platforms combatted stigma, provided mental health support, and amplified marginalized voices. Court support initiatives, like mobilizing sex workers during the Sfiso Mkhwanazi serial killer case, strengthened justice system engagement and visibility through demonstrations and law enforcement sensitization.Regional police dialogues with SARPCCO (Southern Africa Regional Police Chiefs Coordinating Organisation) addressed systemic challenges faced by sex workers in South Africa, Mozambique, and Zimbabwe. Sensitization training improved police attitudes, fostering trust and safer interactions. Advocacy efforts also influenced policymaking, promoting decriminalization and better protections for sex workers. Adopting best practices in police training could reduce violence, improve access to justice, and advance decriminalization efforts—though success depends on political will and resource allocation. Overall, 2023 highlighted both persistent barriers and progress in empowering sex workers through advocacy, research, and creative resistance.Following up on workshops conducted in 2023, a series of engagements were held to assess progress and developments. Meetings were conducted with key networks and organizations, including Platforma in Mozambique, Ungagodoli, and Pathfinder. The objectives were to review advancements in advocacy work, discuss collaborations with law enforcement and healthcare providers, and engage directly with community members. Furthermore, Thought Leaders workshops were facilitated to strengthen movement building and advocacy within the Southern Africa sex worker movement.Significant strides were made in both advocacy and support services. A major focus was on facilitating a law reform summit to discuss policy development and implementation regarding sex work in the SADC region. This informed stakeholders on SRHR issues and strategies for impactful policy change. Concurrently, the development of an online app, GRIT, is underway to provide GBV survivors with accurate information and service access, with co-facilitation from sex workers to ensure its language and accessibility are appropriate.A primary achievement has been the extensive consultative process surrounding the Decriminalization Bill in South Africa. Led by a coalition including Sisonke, SWEAT, and the Asijiki Coalition, these consultations spanned all nine provinces and engaged sex workers of all gender identities. This provided a crucial platform for community members to voice their concerns and shape policy recommendations. The collective input has been instrumental in formulating practical, inclusive recommendations for lawmakers that prioritize the safety, health, and human rights of all individuals involved in sex work.In 2024, the Sisonke national movement conducted the Dignity and Diversity Policing (DDP) sensitisation training. These sessions were designed to educate law enforcement officers, particularly those in the South African Police Service (SAPS), on human rights violations related to sex work and the broader implications for LGBTIQ+ individuals.The program objectives are:•Challenge and transform negative interactions between law enforcement officers and key populations, including sex workers, people who use drugs, and LGBTQ+ communities.•Bridge the gap between law enforcement and key populations by creating a platform for open dialogue, allowing officers to express concerns and gain a deeper understanding of the communities they serve.•Promote diversity, social justice, and cultural sensitivity within SAPS to ensure a more inclusive and human rights-based approach to policing.•Encourage SAPS officers to recognize and address their biases, helping them understand how their actions impact the lives and safety of sex workers and other marginalized groups.•By achieving these objectives, the initiative seeks to foster a more respectful, non-discriminatory, and accountable law enforcement system that upholds the rights and dignity of all individuals.

title.narrative: L1 Key populations effectively use accountability mechanisms towards SRHR
L1 Key populations effectively use accountability mechanisms towards SRHR.

comment.narrative: Currently there is no functioning human rights accountability mechanism at the national level, and efforts to scale up community-led monitoring are underway, but focus on HIV-related services (not SRHR independently).

In 2023, Steering committees have been mobilized to sustain their role in monitoring the implementation of policies committed by the Ministry of Health for the accessibility to services and non-discrimination, and holding implementers accountable. They have been rooting their involvement in the community by coordinating the movements in various regions and looping in feedback for advocacy from the various experiences of individual sex workers. In 2022, Sisonke has implemented outreach actions to ensure documentation of human rights violations and linking sex workers to health services . Through the outreach with Mobile Clinic from partners working on sex work program, Sisonke has ensured that sex workers access the services provided ART treatment and SRHR. The outreach will contribute to serve as a mechanism to monitor human rights violation cases that are reported, to evaluate referrals, and to relay important information to sex workers about organisations that can assist them. Its an ongoing activity to make sure that Sisonke reaches sex workers to gain information on what is happening on the ground. This has a big impact on advocating for the decriminalisation of sex work and SRHR.

comment.narrative: There are not initial CSOs strengthened in order to set up a functional baseline. CSOs will be counted according to the capacity strengthening by taking part of the Love Alliance. South Africa has well-developed civil society and community-led organisations, with communities of sex workers and LGBTIQ+ communities displaying world-class organizing and advocacy. The country’s LGBTIQ+ movement has an estimated 10-15 organisations. Approximately 10% of the organisations are youth-led and 60% refer to women-led CSOs in the country. Despite a restrictive policy environment, sex workers are also well-organised. The community of people who use drugs, while more recent in their organizing, also serves as a regional leader.

Civil society or communit-led organisations are expected to strengthen their financial, governance, administrative or advocacy capacities with the assistance of Sisonke. This refers to the 5-year target

The “Show Me Your Number Community Radio: Sisonke Online Radio Podcast”, is a collaboration between Sisonke and Civil Society Forum. This series of podcasts focus on Health and Human Rights issues for sex workers and how to address these through sports, arts and culture. The podcasts will reach a wide range of people, especially those who have never engaged with sex workers before. One change that was apparent through this activity is that sex workers were able to speak out more and share their lived experiences within the sex work industry. Sisonke’s role was to work with Show Me Your Number Community Radio to train them in the decriminalisation of sex work and create content for the show (audio content), mobilise sex workers to participate (through interviews) and listen to the shows.
